headline: New York sues HUD over housing-counseling funds as $1M state award hangs in balance
dek: The lawsuit challenges the Trump administration’s decision not to award federally approved housing-counseling money, putting services used by thousands of New York households at risk.
body: New York Attorney General Letitia James sued the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development on Wednesday, arguing that the agency unlawfully withheld federal housing-counseling money that supports homeowners, renters and prospective buyers across the state. The case was filed in the Southern District of New York on the final day of the federal fiscal year, when the state said the underlying funds were scheduled to expire. The attorney general’s announcement is at https://ag.ny.gov/press-release/2026/attorney-general-james-sues-trump-administration-protect-housing-counseling-0.

New York is seeking to protect roughly $1 million it applied for through the New York State Housing Finance Agency. The money would be distributed among 22 HUD-certified counseling organizations, with individual grants historically ranging from $20,000 to $100,000. The programs provide guidance on home purchases, rent and mortgage finances, foreclosure prevention, property maintenance and other housing decisions. The state’s complaint says New York has received this federal support regularly for about 13 years and submitted a complete application on May 22, but never received an award or explanation from HUD.

The lawsuit challenges a broader funding decision. The complaint says Congress made approximately $57.5 million available for HUD’s national Housing Counseling program, but HUD had not obligated at least $56.1 million by the time the case was filed. New York argues that federal law requires HUD to make assistance available to approved housing agencies and that Congress did not authorize the department to eliminate or reduce the program on its own. Those are allegations in the state’s complaint, not findings by the court. The filing is available at https://ag.ny.gov/sites/default/files/court-filings/state-of-new-york-v-u.s.-department-of-housing-and-urban-development-complaint-2026.pdf.

The immediate dispute grew out of a September 25 announcement by President Donald Trump seeking to cancel nearly $1 billion in federal spending through a so-called pocket rescission. The Associated Press reported that the package included HUD housing-counseling money along with other programs the administration criticized as unnecessary or ideologically driven: https://apnews.com/article/46b356590699e6225f783c74e7ee3597. In its complaint, New York says the administration’s public criticism focused on the perceived views of some grant recipients rather than the housing services the program funds. HUD and the administration could contest that characterization in court.

The potential impact is more concrete than the statewide grant total. New York’s attorney general says the state’s 2024 funding helped counseling organizations serve more than 7,000 households with one-on-one assistance, provide nearly 2,800 households with financial help to improve living conditions, prevent more than 250 evictions and nearly 300 foreclosures, and help almost 300 first-time buyers close on homes. Those figures describe the prior year’s reported results; they do not establish how many households would lose services immediately if the 2026 grant is not restored.

Housing counseling is designed to help people navigate decisions that can determine whether they remain housed or can buy a home. HUD’s current New York resource page directs residents facing foreclosure or seeking homeownership information to HUD-approved counselors and related assistance: https://www.hud.gov/states/new-york?custom2=0968e9f6-512c-4705-af0f-eb20f79a820f&og1=0968e9f6-512c-4705-af0f-eb20f79a820f. That background helps explain why the funding fight reaches beyond nonprofit budgets: counselors can work with borrowers and tenants before a missed payment, foreclosure filing or failed purchase becomes harder to resolve.

James is asking the court to declare HUD’s actions unlawful, require the department to maintain the program and preserve the unobligated money while the case proceeds. The complaint also asks the court to prevent the funds from being transferred, returned to the Treasury or otherwise made unavailable in a way that would frustrate relief. The filing does not itself restore the grants. The next significant step is a court decision on whether to preserve the money and require HUD to act; until then, New York’s 22 counseling organizations and the households they serve face uncertainty over the state’s expected federal support.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: New York sues HUD over housing counseling funds
seoDescription: New York’s attorney general sued HUD over roughly $1 million in housing-counseling funds for 22 state organizations and thousands of households.
